case: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

Left ventricular myxoma.description: A rare benign primary cardiac tumor composed of myxoid tissue, usually arising in the atria but occasionally in the ventricles. It is often discovered incidentally or can cause embolic or obstructive symptoms.

Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign primary heart tumor made of fibrous tissue, more commonly seen in children but possible in adults. It is often found incidentally and may be located in the ventricles.

Cardiac lipoma.description: A benign tumor composed of mature fat cells that can occur in the myocardium or within cardiac chambers. Many are found incidentally and remain clinically silent.

Papillary fibroelastoma.description: A small benign endocardial tumor, usually arising on valves but occasionally involving other endocardial surfaces. It is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, though it can cause embolic events.

Intracardiac thrombus.description: A blood clot within a cardiac chamber, often associated with ventricular dysfunction, aneurysm, or arrhythmias. It may be found incidentally on imaging and can mimic a tumor.

case: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisy.normalized_text: Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisy
Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisy.description: An infection of the lower part of the left lung that can irritate the pleura, causing pain that worsens with deep breathing or certain positions, along with fever and cough.

Pneumonia with referred abdominal pain.description: Lung infection, especially in the lower lobes, can present with abdominal pain in children because of diaphragmatic irritation and referred pain.

Pleuritis.description: Inflammation of the pleura, often due to infection, causing sharp pain that worsens with breathing or movement and may be accompanied by fever and cough.

Subphrenic abscess.description: A collection of pus beneath the diaphragm that can cause upper abdominal pain, fever, and pain with breathing due to diaphragmatic irritation.

Splenic pathology such as splenic infarc.normalized_text: Splenic pathology such as splenic infarction
Splenic pathology such as splenic infarc.description: A vascular or inflammatory problem involving the spleen can cause left upper quadrant pain and pain with deep breathing or lying down.

case: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

Legionnaires' disease.description: A severe atypical pneumonia caused by Legionella species, often acquired from contaminated water sources and associated with fever, myalgias, respiratory symptoms, and sometimes gastrointestinal complaints.

Melioidosis.description: An infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in parts of Southeast Asia and northern Australia, which can present as pneumonia or disseminated febrile illness with marked inflammatory response.

Scrub typhus.description: A rickettsial infection transmitted by mites, classically causing acute fever, headache, myalgia, and sometimes pneumonitis or systemic inflammation after exposure in endemic regions.

Enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid fever.description: A systemic Salmonella infection acquired through contaminated food or water, causing prolonged fever and gastrointestinal symptoms, sometimes with myalgia and abdominal discomfort.

Community-acquired pneumonia with pleuri.description: An acute lower respiratory tract infection that can cause fever, tachypnoea, pleuritic chest or diaphragmatic pain, and systemic inflammatory markers, though imaging may initially be normal.

case: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause gradually progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, bladder dysfunction, and visual impairment.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic neuropathy
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness, sometimes accompanied by optic atrophy or other neurologic features.

Mitochondrial optic neuropathy / Leber h.normalized_text: Mitochondrial optic neuropathy / Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)-plus syndrome
Mitochondrial optic neuropathy / Leber h.description: A mitochondrial disorder that classically causes subacute or progressive central visual loss, but can also be associated with additional neurologic manifestations such as spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, or parkinsonism.

Adrenomyeloneuropathy.description: An X-linked disorder of very-long-chain fatty acid metabolism causing progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction, usually with adrenal involvement and often in men.

case: A 14-year-old female patient presented with generalized pruritus accompanied by scleral icterus and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for over 2 months. She had no fever, abdominal pain, or distension. Past medical history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had been taking Chinese herbal medicines (specific components unknown) for approximately 9 months. Physical examination revealed clear consciousness, facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound tenderness, and no lower extremity edema.

Herb-induced cholestatic hepatitis.description: Drug- or supplement-related liver injury that impairs bile flow, leading to cholestatic jaundice and pruritus; herbal products are a well-known cause of idiosyncratic liver injury.

Autoimmune hepatitis with cholestatic fe.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that can cause jaundice, impaired liver synthetic function, and secondary bruising; some patients may have cholestatic symptoms such as itching.

Primary biliary cholangitis.description: A chronic autoimmune disease of the small intrahepatic bile ducts that classically causes pruritus and jaundice due to cholestasis.

Biliary obstruction / extrahepatic chole.description: Blockage of bile flow from the liver to the intestine, which can produce pruritus and jaundice; causes include stones, strictures, or masses.

Chronic liver disease with hepatic synth.normalized_text: Chronic liver disease with hepatic synthetic dysfunction
Chronic liver disease with hepatic synth.description: Longstanding liver injury from various causes can reduce clotting factor production and hormone metabolism, leading to jaundice, bruising, and menstrual irregularities.

case: A 66-year-old man presented with 2 days of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. His history included hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; azathioprine 75 mg had been started 10 days earlier. On examination, he was febrile (38°C) with bilateral tender knees and a patellar tap. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated CRP and ESR, mildly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, dsDNA, ENA, and anti-ASO tests. Renal function and urinalysis were normal, chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

Azathioprine-induced serum sickness-like.description: An immune-mediated drug reaction that can occur after exposure to a new medication, causing fever, rash, and joint pains, often within days to weeks of starting therapy.

Drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (.description: A severe medication-related hypersensitivity syndrome that typically presents with fever, rash, and systemic inflammation after a new drug exposure.

Reactive arthritis.description: An inflammatory arthritis that usually follows an infection and can cause joint pain and swelling with systemic symptoms.

Acute viral exanthem with viral arthralg.normalized_text: Acute viral exanthem with viral arthralgia
Acute viral exanthem with viral arthralg.description: A viral illness that can cause fever, rash, malaise, and joint pains, sometimes mimicking autoimmune or drug reactions.

Rheumatoid arthritis flare or early infl.normalized_text: Rheumatoid arthritis flare or early inflammatory arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis flare or early infl.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that can present with joint pain, swelling, and elevated inflammatory markers.

case: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.

Blunt laryngeal trauma with possible lar.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal trauma with possible laryngeal fracture
Blunt laryngeal trauma with possible lar.description: Injury to the larynx after direct blunt neck trauma can cause swelling, voice changes, dysphagia, and airway compromise; severe cases may include cartilage fracture or internal laryngeal edema/hematoma.

Retropharyngeal hematoma.description: A collection of blood in the retropharyngeal space after trauma can expand over time and compress the airway, causing dysphagia, hoarseness, and neck swelling.

Anterior neck soft tissue contusion with.normalized_text: Anterior neck soft tissue contusion with hematoma
Anterior neck soft tissue contusion with.description: Blunt trauma to the soft tissues of the neck can cause bruising, swelling, pain with movement, and secondary airway concerns if edema extends to deeper structures.

Pharyngeal edema from blunt neck trauma.normalized_text: Pharyngeal edema from blunt neck trauma
Pharyngeal edema from blunt neck trauma.description: Trauma can produce inflammatory swelling of the pharyngeal tissues, including the posterior pharyngeal wall, which may narrow the airway and cause swallowing or voice symptoms.

Cervical spine injury unlikely but consi.normalized_text: Cervical spine injury unlikely but considered in neck trauma
Cervical spine injury unlikely but consi.description: Trauma to the neck can sometimes involve the cervical spine, which may present with neck pain and movement limitation, though neurologic findings are often more prominent.

case: 37-year-old man with 3 months of episodic weakness, irritability, poor concentration, sweet cravings, foggy sensorium, cold clammy feeling, fatigue, strange behavior, and memory loss, occurring especially after several hours without eating and at night/early morning. He gained 30 lb from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. Past history was unremarkable except umbilical hernia repair and back surgery 10 years earlier; no medication use, no smoking or illicit drugs, social alcohol use, and family history of diabetes. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy; other system examinations were unremarkable. Routine labs, glycated hemoglobin, adrenal testing, calcium, and pituitary/thyroid hormones were largely normal except mildly elevated prolactin. MR cholangiopancreatography showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion arising from the anterior pancreas between the head and neck.

Insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin inappropriately, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenic and adrenergic symptoms.

Factitious hypoglycemia due to exogenous.normalized_text: Factitious hypoglycemia due to exogenous insulin or sulfonylurea use
Factitious hypoglycemia due to exogenous.description: Self-induced or accidental hypoglycemia caused by insulin administration or insulin secretagogues, typically producing recurrent low-glucose episodes that improve with eating.

Other functional pancreatic neuroendocri.description: A hormone-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor other than insulinoma; depending on the hormone produced, these tumors can cause variable systemic symptoms and may appear as hypervascular pancreatic lesions.

case: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation of the costochondral or costosternal joints that causes localized anterior chest wall pain, often worsened by movement, exercise, or palpation.

Intercostal or abdominal wall muscle str.normalized_text: Intercostal or abdominal wall muscle strain
Intercostal or abdominal wall muscle str.description: Overuse injury of the intercostal or adjacent abdominal muscles, commonly caused by repetitive exertion or new exercise routines and producing movement-related localized pain.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Hypermobility of the lower costal cartilages causing intermittent sharp chest or upper abdominal pain, often provoked by twisting, bending, or core exercises.

Pectoralis minor/major strain.description: Muscle strain in the chest wall from repetitive resistance training or abrupt increases in exercise intensity, causing localized pain that is worse with contraction.

case: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

Colonic lipoma.description: A benign fatty tumor of the colon that is often found incidentally and may cause no symptoms when small.

Colorectal adenoma (adenomatous polyp).description: A precancerous glandular polyp of the colon or rectum that is frequently asymptomatic and discovered during screening examinations.

Early colorectal carcinoma.description: An early-stage malignant tumor of the large bowel that can be detected incidentally before symptoms or laboratory abnormalities appear.

case: A 67-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 4-month history of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea that had initially been diagnosed as eosinophilic asthma at another hospital, with symptoms worsening despite treatment with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. He had no smoking history and unremarkable medical history. On examination, he required 1L nasal cannula oxygen with SaO2 of 96%, had decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field with fine crackles, and no raised JVP, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right ground glass opacities, and high-resolution CT revealed ground glass opacities surrounded by consolidation in the right lower lung field.

Organizing pneumonia (cryptogenic or sec.description: An inflammatory lung disease characterized by granulation tissue filling small airways and alveoli, often causing subacute cough, dyspnea, and patchy ground-glass or consolidative opacities on imaging.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophil-rich inflammatory lung disorder that often presents with cough, dyspnea, wheezing, and peripheral or patchy infiltrates, frequently responsive to corticosteroids.

Primary lung adenocarcinoma, including l.normalized_text: Primary lung adenocarcinoma, including lepidic-predominant pattern
Primary lung adenocarcinoma, including l.description: A common non-small cell lung cancer that can present with persistent cough, dyspnea, and ground-glass or consolidative opacities, sometimes mimicking pneumonia or inflammatory lung disease.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.description: An immune-mediated interstitial lung disease caused by inhaled environmental antigens, leading to cough, dyspnea, crackles, and ground-glass changes on imaging.

Asthma with poor control or atypical adu.normalized_text: Asthma with poor control or atypical adult-onset asthma
Asthma with poor control or atypical adu.description: A chronic inflammatory airway disease causing episodic wheezing, cough, and dyspnea, usually improving with bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids.

case: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn diseas.description: A chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract that can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, growth failure, and systemic inflammation.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculous infection of the gastrointestinal tract, often involving the ileocecal region, causing chronic abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, anemia, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Acute leukemia.description: A malignancy of blood-forming cells that can present with fever, pallor, fatigue, bruising, abdominal pain from organ enlargement, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Amebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica colitis.description: An intestinal parasitic infection that can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, dysentery, fever, and weight loss, especially after travel to endemic regions.

Hookworm infection.description: A parasitic intestinal infection acquired from contaminated soil that can cause chronic blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anemia, pallor, abdominal discomfort, and weakness.

case: A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department during the summer with a 4-day history of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, and fatigue following his return from a 2-week trip to East Africa. During his trip to Tanzania, he had been on safari without animal contact but received mosquito bites, especially during the first days. He consumed cooked shrimp and lobster and a small amount of raw tuna. On the second-to-last day of the trip, he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Upon returning to Massachusetts, he experienced fever (38.3°C to 39.5°C), shaking chills, diffuse headache, and lower back pain. He reported weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes. His medical history included degenerative knee disease with previous glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he had a temperature of 38.9°C, blood pressure 113/62 mm Hg, facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: A mosquito-borne parasitic infection that can cause high fevers, chills, headache, hemolysis, jaundice, dark urine, and severe systemic illness after travel to endemic areas.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne parasitic infection of red blood cells that causes fever, chills, hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and dark urine, especially in immunocompromised patients.

Leptospirosis.description: A bacterial zoonotic infection acquired from water or soil contaminated with animal urine; it can cause fever, headache, myalgias, jaundice, renal dysfunction, and dark urine.

Severe viral or bacterial traveler's gas.normalized_text: Severe viral or bacterial traveler's gastroenteritis with dehydration
Severe viral or bacterial traveler's gas.description: An acute infectious gastrointestinal illness acquired during travel that can cause vomiting, diarrhea, fever, weakness, and dehydration; severe dehydration can lead to dark urine and reduced urine output.

case: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

Paraspinal abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in the muscles and soft tissues adjacent to the spine, usually due to bacterial infection and often associated with fever and pain.

Spinal epidural abscess.description: An accumulation of pus in the epidural space around the spinal cord, typically caused by bacterial infection and presenting with pain, fever, and possible neurologic deficits.

Cervical vertebral osteomyelitis.description: Infection of the cervical vertebral bone, often caused by hematogenous spread or contiguous extension from nearby infection, leading to pain and systemic symptoms.

Infected cervical spine hardware.description: Infection involving implanted spinal instrumentation, which can cause deep neck pain, fever, and formation of adjacent abscesses.

Deep neck space infection.description: A bacterial infection in the deep fascial spaces of the neck that can present with pain, swallowing difficulty, fever, and may extend into adjacent structures.

case: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal perforati.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus, classically caused by forceful vomiting and associated with sudden severe chest pain, often radiating to the back, and signs of systemic illness.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A life-threatening tear in the aortic wall causing sudden severe chest pain that often radiates to the back and may present with diaphoresis and tachycardia.

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS).description: Reduced blood flow to the heart, typically causing chest pain and autonomic symptoms such as sweating, nausea, and vomiting.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas that can cause severe upper abdominal or chest pain radiating to the back, with nausea and vomiting.

Mallory-Weiss tear.description: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by forceful retching or vomiting, usually presenting with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

case: 27-year-old man with 2 years of recurrent convulsive episodes: trunk/arm/leg shaking lasting 4–8 minutes, often preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Episodes increased in frequency to about weekly despite levetiracetam; one event was associated with urinary incontinence, and another was witnessed as shaking with clenching movements. On examination, he was awake and alert but nonverbal, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and extremities. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included febrile seizure in childhood, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Labs were largely normal except mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES).description: Seizure-like episodes caused by functional/psychological factors rather than abnormal electrical activity in the brain; often associated with trauma-related and psychiatric conditions.

Epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-c.description: A neurologic disorder characterized by recurrent unprovoked seizures that may begin focally and spread to generalized convulsions.

Syncope with convulsive movements (convu.description: Transient cerebral hypoperfusion can cause fainting with brief tonic or jerking movements that may resemble a seizure.

Pancreatic nonepileptic paroxysmal event.normalized_text: Pancreatic nonepileptic paroxysmal events related to panic disorder
Pancreatic nonepileptic paroxysmal event.description: Panic attacks can produce intense autonomic symptoms and shaking that may be mistaken for seizures, especially in patients with anxiety and trauma histories.

Post-traumatic epilepsy.description: Epilepsy that develops after head trauma, with recurrent seizures arising from prior brain injury.

case: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

Obturator hernia.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal, often causing small-bowel obstruction and pain that may radiate to the medial thigh or knee (Howship-Romberg sign).

Strangulated small-bowel obstruction due.normalized_text: Strangulated small-bowel obstruction due to internal hernia
Strangulated small-bowel obstruction due.description: An obstruction caused by bowel trapped through an internal defect, which can lead to abdominal distension, vomiting, and pain; strangulation may be subtle early on.

Inguinal or femoral hernia with bowel ob.normalized_text: Inguinal or femoral hernia with bowel obstruction
Inguinal or femoral hernia with bowel ob.description: A hernia through the groin or femoral canal can trap bowel and cause intestinal obstruction, especially in older, frail women.

Acute gout or pseudogout of the knee.normalized_text: Acute gout or pseudogout of the knee
Acute gout or pseudogout of the knee.description: An inflammatory crystal arthritis that commonly causes sudden joint pain, swelling, and tenderness, usually in an older adult.

case: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsened 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1 day of left-eye visual disturbance and visual field defect, and 2 days later developed sudden left-sided hearing loss. Three weeks later, she had a right-eye visual field defect, followed by tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic disease, cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy. On examination, pupils were reactive without relative afferent pupillary defect; visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg bilaterally; anterior segment exam was normal. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP were normal. CSF showed mildly elevated protein (74.4 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands, and no specific hematologic or rheumatologic abnormalities were found.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare immune-mediated microangiopathy that affects the brain, retina, and inner ear, classically causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune thrombophilia that causes arterial or venous thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity, and can lead to retinal or cerebral ischemic events.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause visual symptoms, sensory deficits, and other neurologic complaints.

Meniere disease.description: An inner ear disorder characterized by episodic sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness, and vertigo due to endolymphatic hydrops.

Optic neuritis.description: Inflammation of the optic nerve that typically causes painful monocular vision loss, decreased color vision, and an afferent pupillary defect.

case: 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture and gradually progressed to gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor balance with tandem gait, and no limb ataxia; MMSE was 25. Labs showed elevated creatine kinase, normal resting blood and CSF lactate, low TSH, elevated antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mildly positive ANA. EMG showed mild myopathic changes. Audiometry revealed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

Mitochondrial myopathy / multisystem mit.description: A disorder of mitochondrial energy production that can cause slowly progressive muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, ataxia, hearing loss, cardiac rhythm abnormalities, and mild cognitive changes.

Inclusion body myositis.description: A chronic inflammatory myopathy in older adults causing slowly progressive muscle weakness, often with weakness of the quadriceps, finger flexors, and sometimes neck muscles, and a mildly elevated CK.

Multiple system atrophy, cerebellar type.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia and gait imbalance, often with autonomic dysfunction and variable parkinsonian features.

Autoimmune thyroid-associated myopathy.description: Muscle weakness and myopathic symptoms associated with thyroid dysfunction or autoimmune thyroid disease, sometimes with elevated CK and positive thyroid antibodies.

Spinocerebellar ataxia with myopathy (ge.normalized_text: Spinocerebellar ataxia with myopathy (genetic ataxia-myopathy syndrome)
Spinocerebellar ataxia with myopathy (ge.description: A hereditary neurologic syndrome in which cerebellar degeneration occurs together with muscle involvement, producing gait ataxia and weakness that can progress over years.

case: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Primary bone diffuse large B-cell lympho.normalized_text: Primary bone diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
Primary bone diffuse large B-cell lympho.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can present as a localized mass in bone or soft tissue with pain and regional lymphadenopathy.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma in children that often presents with rapidly growing mass lesions and may involve extranodal sites.

Primary bone lymphoma, unspecified matur.normalized_text: Primary bone lymphoma, unspecified mature B-cell type
Primary bone lymphoma, unspecified matur.description: A lymphoma originating in bone or adjacent soft tissue, often causing localized pain, swelling, and sometimes regional node enlargement.

Lymphoblastic lymphoma / acute lymphobla.normalized_text: Lymphoblastic lymphoma / acute lymphoblastic leukemia, B-cell type
Lymphoblastic lymphoma / acute lymphobla.description: A precursor lymphoid malignancy that commonly affects children and can present with lymphadenopathy, masses, anemia, and bone pain.

Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma.normalized_text: Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma or other mature small B-cell lymphoma
Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma.description: A usually indolent mature B-cell lymphoma that can involve extranodal sites and present with a localized mass and nodes, though it is uncommon in very young children.

case: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.description: A chronic parasitic liver disease caused by Schistosoma mansoni, leading to intestinal infection and hepatic periportal inflammation/fibrosis; it can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fever, and may produce abnormal liver imaging findings.

Schistosomal hepatic pseudotumor / focal.normalized_text: Schistosomal hepatic pseudotumor / focal hepatic granuloma
Schistosomal hepatic pseudotumor / focal.description: A mass-like liver lesion caused by inflammatory granulomatous reaction to schistosome eggs, sometimes mimicking a tumor or abscess on ultrasound or CT.

Amebic liver abscess.description: A protozoal infection of the liver, usually presenting with fever and right upper quadrant pain, often in children or adults from endemic regions; imaging is commonly used for diagnosis.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial abscess in the liver that typically causes prolonged fever, abdominal pain, and inflammatory signs; ultrasound and CT are often ordered to evaluate it.

Post-traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver.normalized_text: Post-traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver injury
Post-traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver.description: Bleeding or contusion in the liver following abdominal trauma, which can cause right upper quadrant pain and prompt imaging studies.

case: 44-year-old man with 1 month of intermittent, nonexertional substernal burning chest pain lasting hours to days and partially relieved by antacids/omeprazole, presenting with a 1-hour episode of severe pain radiating to the left arm, associated with nausea and nonbloody vomiting. He denied dyspnea, fever, cough, trauma, edema, or immobility. Past history was unremarkable, with no tobacco, alcohol, or drug use and no family history of premature coronary disease. He reported a previously noted elevated platelet count (~600,000/mm³) 12 years earlier and intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers, without prior bleeding, thrombosis, headache, dizziness, or neurologic symptoms. Exam showed distress but was otherwise unremarkable: afebrile, blood pressure 133/83 mmHg, heart rate 61 bpm, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, regular cardiac rhythm, no JVD or edema, clear lungs, and nontender chest and abdomen. Labs showed troponin 0.08 ng/mL, WBC 22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia, platelets 771,000/mm³, hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, and glucose 192 mg/dL.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute coronary syndrome (non-ST-elevatio.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome (non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction / unstable angina)
Acute coronary syndrome (non-ST-elevatio.description: A partial or complete reduction in blood flow to the heart muscle causing chest pain and myocardial injury; NSTEMI typically has elevated troponin without ST-elevation.

Essential thrombocythemia.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent overproduction of platelets, increasing risk of arterial and venous thrombosis and microvascular symptoms.

Polycythemia vera.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm causing increased red blood cell mass, often with elevated platelets and white cells; it can cause pruritus after hot showers and thrombosis.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) /.description: Acid reflux causing burning retrosternal discomfort, often improved by antacids or proton pump inhibitors; severe episodes can mimic cardiac pain.

case: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Pregnancy was complicated by maternal hepatitis C infection, treated Chlamydia trachomatis infection, gestational hypertension, and prenatal right urinary tract dilatation on serial ultrasound from 20 weeks to term. At 40 weeks, after prolonged labor and cesarean delivery for nonreassuring fetal status with meconium-stained amniotic fluid, she was born in breech position with limp tone and no respiratory effort. She required 16 minutes of resuscitation with intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses before return of circulation. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU arrival, she was hypothermic (34.9°C), with heart rate 141 bpm, blood pressure 84/59 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on mechanical ventilation; therapeutic hypothermia was started.

Severe perinatal asphyxia / hypoxic-isch.description: Brain injury caused by inadequate oxygen and blood flow around the time of birth, often following fetal distress, prolonged labor, or difficult delivery. It commonly leads to poor tone, apnea, low Apgar scores, and need for extensive resuscitation, and may be treated with therapeutic hypothermia.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Respiratory distress caused by inhalation of meconium-stained amniotic fluid before or during birth, which can obstruct airways and impair gas exchange. It often occurs after fetal distress or post-term delivery and may require intensive ventilatory support.

Neonatal depression secondary to difficu.normalized_text: Neonatal depression secondary to difficult delivery
Neonatal depression secondary to difficu.description: Transient severe neonatal depression after a complicated birth, characterized by poor tone, apnea, bradycardia or absent circulation, and the need for resuscitation. It can result from prolonged labor, fetal distress, or operative delivery complications.

Neonatal encephalopathy.description: A clinical syndrome of disturbed neurologic function in the newborn, usually presenting with altered consciousness, abnormal tone, seizures, or poor feeding, often due to hypoxic-ischemic injury but also from other causes.

Congenital hydronephrosis / antenatal ur.normalized_text: Congenital hydronephrosis / antenatal urinary tract obstruction
Congenital hydronephrosis / antenatal ur.description: Dilation of the fetal renal collecting system detected on prenatal ultrasound, which may be due to transient hydronephrosis, vesicoureteral reflux, or urinary tract obstruction. Severity ranges from benign to clinically significant renal disease.

case: 54-year-old man with polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive, with distended jugular veins and bibasilar crackles. Labs showed severe renal failure (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL), proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.9), elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, and persistently low C3 with normal C4. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and metabolites. Blood and urine cultures were negative, and kidney ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm. Family history was notable for a sister with renal failure requiring dialysis at age 45.

C3 glomerulopathy (C3 glomerulonephritis.normalized_text: C3 glomerulopathy (C3 glomerulonephritis / dense deposit disease)
C3 glomerulopathy (C3 glomerulonephritis.description: A complement-mediated kidney disease caused by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, leading to low C3, proteinuria, hematuria, and progressive chronic kidney failure.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.normalized_text: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy)
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (comp.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy due to complement pathway dysregulation, causing kidney injury, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and sometimes severe hypertension.

Malignant hypertension with thrombotic m.description: A hypertensive emergency that can cause end-organ damage, acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, and microangiopathic hemolysis.

Hepatitis C–associated membranoprolifera.description: An immune-complex glomerulonephritis associated with chronic hepatitis C, often presenting with proteinuria, low complement, and progressive kidney dysfunction.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.normalized_text: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy / renal ischemic injury
Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: Cocaine can trigger severe vasoconstriction, malignant hypertension, and kidney injury, sometimes with a thrombotic microangiopathy pattern.

case: 44-year-old Chinese woman, previously healthy, with a 7-week history of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting and 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. She received antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics for 3 weeks without improvement. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, absent pharyngeal reflex, decreased right tendon reflexes, and bilateral Babinski sign. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glycemic tests; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that can present with intractable nausea and vomiting from involvement of the medulla/area postrema and later develop brainstem or spinal cord deficits.

Brainstem encephalitis involving the dor.normalized_text: Brainstem encephalitis involving the dorsal medulla/area postrema
Brainstem encephalitis involving the dor.description: Inflammation of the brainstem, especially the dorsal medulla, can cause intractable vomiting, ocular movement abnormalities, dysphagia, and long-tract signs.

Area postrema syndrome.description: A clinical syndrome caused by dysfunction of the area postrema in the medulla, classically producing unexplained intractable nausea, vomiting, and hiccups; it is often an initial presentation of NMOSD.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause brainstem symptoms and motor deficits, though isolated prolonged vomiting is less common.

Posterior fossa or brainstem lesion.description: A structural lesion such as tumor, stroke, or compression in the posterior fossa/brainstem can cause vomiting, nystagmus, cranial nerve dysfunction, and long-tract signs.

case: 47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. Physical examination revealed aortic valve diastolic murmurs at the precordium.

Subacute infective endocarditis.description: A bacterial infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, often affecting damaged valves and causing a prolonged, nonspecific systemic illness.

Aortic valve disease with aortic regurgi.normalized_text: Aortic valve disease with aortic regurgitation
Aortic valve disease with aortic regurgi.description: Structural or functional disease of the aortic valve that can cause a diastolic murmur and symptoms related to reduced cardiac efficiency.

Systemic viral illness.description: A generalized viral infection or post-viral syndrome that can produce prolonged constitutional symptoms such as fever, body aches, and fatigue.

Autoimmune inflammatory disease (e.g., c.normalized_text: Autoimmune inflammatory disease (e.g., connective tissue disease or vasculitis)
Autoimmune inflammatory disease (e.g., c.description: A noninfectious immune-mediated disorder that can cause chronic fever, fatigue, muscle and joint pain, and other systemic symptoms.

case: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

Paradoxical embolism.description: An embolus from the venous circulation crosses into the arterial circulation through an intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt, causing systemic ischemic events such as stroke or myocardial infarction.

Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.normalized_text: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic embolization
Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.description: Air enters the venous system, often during a procedure, and can obstruct pulmonary circulation or pass through a right-to-left shunt into the arterial system, causing neurologic and cardiac ischemic symptoms.

Acute myocardial infarction.description: Myocardial necrosis due to acute coronary artery ischemia, typically presenting with crushing chest pain and elevated cardiac biomarkers, sometimes with ECG changes.

Transient ischemic attack / embolic isch.normalized_text: Transient ischemic attack / embolic ischemic stroke
Transient ischemic attack / embolic isch.description: A brief episode of focal neurologic dysfunction caused by temporary cerebral ischemia, often due to embolism, with symptoms resolving fully within 24 hours.

Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left.normalized_text: Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunt
Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left.description: A persistent interatrial communication that can allow venous blood or emboli to bypass the lungs and enter the systemic circulation, especially during transient increases in right atrial pressure.

case: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.description: A usually slow-growing, superficial glial tumor of young people, often presenting with seizures and headaches; commonly associated with BRAF V600E mutation.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A higher-grade, more aggressive variant of PXA that can present similarly to grade 2 PXA but tends to have a more rapid course and recurrence risk.

Ganglioglioma.description: A typically low-grade neuronal-glial tumor that often occurs in younger patients and commonly causes epilepsy and headaches.

Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (.description: A benign epilepsy-associated brain tumor, usually low-grade, often presenting with long-standing focal seizures in children or young adults.

case: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous skin rash and progressive muscle weakness. The rash began on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees, followed one week later by generalized myalgias and worsening weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Prior examination showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema, erythematous papules on the fingertips, and moderate-to-severe bilateral weakness of the deltoids, triceps, hip flexors, hamstrings, and quadriceps, with normal muscle bulk, tone, reflexes, and sensation. On exam at this hospital, he had bilateral heliotrope rash, erythematous papules on the extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees, periungual erythema, pitting edema of the arms and legs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, hypoactive bowel sounds, and marked proximal weakness with inability to lift his arms, legs, or head against gravity. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive skin findings such as heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; it may also be associated with interstitial lung disease, edema, and malignancy.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal muscle weakness without the characteristic skin manifestations of dermatomyositis.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune overlap syndrome often associated with inflammatory myopathy, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and mechanic's hands; it can overlap with dermatomyositis features.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy that causes rapidly progressive proximal weakness and high muscle injury, often associated with statin exposure or specific autoantibodies; skin findings are usually absent.

case: A 59-year-old woman presented with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures, for which she had been using phenytoin for more than 20 years. She was referred with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness, associated with generalized bone and muscle pain, resulting in significant limitations in her daily activities. Her symptoms had further worsened with progressive proximal muscle pain and weakness and increasing bone pain. Physical examination revealed normal renal and liver function. Conventional radiographs demonstrated Looser's zones in the femoral neck bilaterally.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: A bone-softening disorder caused by long-term phenytoin therapy, which can impair vitamin D metabolism and lead to defective bone mineralization.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: A disorder of impaired bone mineralization due to insufficient vitamin D, often presenting with bone pain, muscle weakness, and pseudofractures.

Anticonvulsant-induced bone disease.description: A spectrum of bone disorders seen in patients taking long-term antiepileptic drugs, commonly involving reduced bone density, osteomalacia, and fracture risk.

Hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.description: A form of osteomalacia caused by low serum phosphate, resulting in defective mineralization, bone pain, weakness, and pseudofractures.

case: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

Infective endocarditis with septic embol.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with septic embolic stroke
Infective endocarditis with septic embol.description: Infection of the heart valves or endocardial surface that can cause fever, a new or worsening murmur, heart failure, and embolic events such as stroke.

Acute ischemic stroke from cardioembolis.description: An acute interruption of blood flow to part of the brain, often causing sudden focal neurologic deficits such as dysarthria or limb incoordination.

Acute mitral regurgitation due to valvul.normalized_text: Acute mitral regurgitation due to valvular infection or rupture
Acute mitral regurgitation due to valvul.description: Sudden failure of the mitral valve to close properly, leading to a loud systolic murmur, pulmonary congestion, and signs of heart failure.

Rheumatic carditis.description: An inflammatory cardiac complication of recent group A streptococcal infection that can cause valvulitis and murmurs, usually as part of acute rheumatic fever.

case: Patient 1: 3.5-year-old male from unrelated Polish parents. Born at 39 weeks gestation with birth weight 3700g (50th-75th centile), length 57cm (97th centile), head circumference 36cm (75th-97th centile), thorax circumference 33cm (25-50th centile), Apgar score 9 at 1 min. Family history unremarkable. Proteinuria, hematuria and glycosuria noted in early neonatal period. UTI at 12 months. At 3 years developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine. Laboratory investigations showed constant proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, eGFR (Schwartz) 30.56 ml/min/1.73 m2, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglyceride; normal CBC, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid and liver function tests. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortex echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Normal male karyotype (46,XY).

Nephropathic cystinosis.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder causing proximal renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome) and progressive chronic kidney disease in infancy or early childhood.

Dent disease.description: An X-linked proximal renal tubular disorder characterized by low-molecular-weight proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, and progressive kidney disease in boys.

Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrom.description: An X-linked disorder causing proximal renal tubular Fanconi syndrome, congenital cataracts, hypotonia, and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Fanconi syndrome.description: A generalized proximal renal tubular reabsorption defect leading to urinary loss of glucose, proteins, and other filtered solutes, often causing chronic kidney disease if persistent.

Congenital nephrotic syndrome.description: A group of inherited kidney disorders causing heavy proteinuria very early in life, often leading to hypoalbuminemia and progressive renal impairment.

case: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive skin rash; in adults it can be associated with an underlying malignancy.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory muscle disease causing progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, typically without the characteristic rash seen in dermatomyositis.

Paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy.description: An inflammatory muscle syndrome triggered by an underlying cancer, often presenting like dermatomyositis with weakness, rash, and elevated muscle enzymes.

Necrotizing autoimmune myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disease causing rapid proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase levels; skin rash is usually absent and dysphagia may occur.

case: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: A childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head that typically causes progressive hip pain, limp, and restricted hip motion in school-aged children.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A self-limited inflammatory condition of the hip synovium that commonly causes limp and hip pain in children, often after a viral illness.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: A displacement of the femoral head through the growth plate, usually in adolescents, causing limp, hip or knee pain, and limited internal rotation.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A serious joint infection causing acute pain, limp, limited motion, and usually systemic illness with fever.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis.description: A chronic inflammatory arthritis of childhood that can involve the hip and cause limp, pain, and limited range of motion.

case: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.

Perforated peptic ulcer.description: A hole in the stomach or duodenal wall that causes sudden contamination of the abdominal cavity, leading to peritonitis, fever, and severe abdominal pain.

Subphrenic abscess.description: A collection of pus beneath the diaphragm, often occurring after abdominal surgery or intra-abdominal infection, causing fever, abdominal pain, and inflammatory markers.

Acute cholangitis.description: Infection of the bile ducts, usually due to biliary obstruction, classically causing fever, right upper quadrant pain, and systemic inflammatory response.

Adhesive small bowel obstruction.description: Mechanical bowel obstruction caused by intra-abdominal adhesions, commonly after prior surgery, leading to abdominal pain and vomiting.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Inflammation of the pancreas that typically causes upper abdominal pain, vomiting, and systemic inflammatory signs.

case: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

Cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.normalized_text: Cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion syndrome)
Cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal deletion disorder caused by loss of part of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a cat-like high-pitched cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, and characteristic facial features.

5p deletion syndrome with congenital hea.normalized_text: 5p deletion syndrome with congenital heart disease
5p deletion syndrome with congenital hea.description: A broader description of partial deletion of chromosome 5p causing neurodevelopmental impairment, growth and craniofacial abnormalities, and occasional congenital malformations such as heart defects.

Congenital developmental delay with micr.description: A non-specific neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by delayed milestones and reduced head circumference, which can result from many genetic or structural causes.

case: 7-year-old girl with no past medical history, presenting with intermittent abdominal pain for about 1 month, unrelieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated at 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasound demonstrated multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes; pelvic organs were unremarkable. Surgical resection revealed a 4 cm jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the jejunum, with reactive hyperplasia in sampled lymph nodes.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary extra-gonadal yolk sac tumor of.normalized_text: Primary extra-gonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
Primary extra-gonadal yolk sac tumor of.description: A malignant germ cell tumor that can arise outside the gonads and often produces alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). In the bowel it is rare, but can present as an invasive abdominal mass with nodal involvement.

Nonseminomatous germ cell tumor with yol.normalized_text: Nonseminomatous germ cell tumor with yolk sac differentiation
Nonseminomatous germ cell tumor with yol.description: A germ cell malignancy composed of nonseminomatous elements, often secreting AFP. These tumors can occur in extragonadal sites and may present with abdominal masses and lymphadenopathy.

Small bowel adenocarcinoma producing AFP.description: A rare malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine. Some poorly differentiated tumors can produce AFP and present with abdominal pain, bowel-wall masses, and regional spread.

Malignant lymphoma of the small bowel.normalized_text: Malignant lymphoma of the small bowel
Malignant lymphoma of the small bowel.description: A lymphoid malignancy that can involve the intestine and abdominal lymph nodes, causing abdominal pain and bowel-wall masses or thickening.

case: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent, severe abdominal pain waking him from sleep, associated with crying, leg flexion toward the chest, and episodic abdominal rigidity. He developed three bowel movements with progressively increasing red blood, the last nearly all blood with a large clot. History includes infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and is on low-lactose cow milk-based formula. On examination, he had diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, later pallor, with no abdominal mass or anal fissure. Initial vitals showed tachycardia and low blood pressure.

Intussusception.description: A segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, causing intermittent intestinal obstruction, ischemia, and sometimes bleeding. It is common in infants and often presents with episodic severe pain and bloody stool.

Malrotation with midgut volvulus.description: An abnormal intestinal rotation that predisposes the midgut to twist around the mesenteric vessels, causing bowel obstruction and ischemia. It is a surgical emergency and can present with severe abdominal pain and shock.

Meckel diverticulum with gastrointestina.description: A congenital remnant of the vitelline duct that can contain ectopic gastric mucosa and cause painless or sometimes painful lower gastrointestinal bleeding in young children.

Anal fissure.description: A small tear in the anal mucosa that commonly causes bright red blood with stools in infants, often associated with painful defecation.

case: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Constrictive bronchiolitis (bronchioliti.description: A disease of the small airways causing fixed airflow obstruction due to inflammation and scarring of the bronchioles.

Severe asthma with fixed airflow obstruc.normalized_text: Severe asthma with fixed airflow obstruction
Severe asthma with fixed airflow obstruc.description: A chronic inflammatory airway disease that can lead to persistent obstruction and marked reduction in expiratory flow.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) unrelated to smoking
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.description: A chronic disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation, sometimes caused by non-smoking exposures such as biomass smoke, occupational dusts, or prior lung injury.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with bronch.description: An immune-mediated lung disease caused by inhaled environmental antigens that can involve the small airways and produce obstructive physiology.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency-related e.description: A genetic cause of early or severe obstructive lung disease due to unchecked protease activity leading to emphysema and airflow limitation.

case: 27-year-old man previously healthy, with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. Past history notable for left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that had enlarged and regressed spontaneously since age 15. On examination, he was thin (168 cm, 48 kg), with low-grade fever (37.6°C), mild hypoxemia (SpO2 94% on room air), left upper lung crackles, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures and serologic tests for bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, autoimmune, HIV, and tumor markers were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identified pathogens.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often affecting the lungs and lymph nodes.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can produce cough, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous inflammation.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoma that often presents with painless lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms; it can rarely involve the lungs and cause inflammatory markers to rise.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection.description: An infection caused by environmental mycobacteria that can produce chronic pulmonary disease and granulomatous inflammation.

Endemic fungal infection causing granulo.normalized_text: Endemic fungal infection causing granulomatous lung disease
Endemic fungal infection causing granulo.description: A fungal infection such as histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis that can cause pulmonary symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and granulomas.

case: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. He presented with leukopenia (0.83 × 10^9/L) at hospital admission.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A rare, often fatal demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC virus, typically seen in immunosuppressed patients. It can produce focal neurological deficits, visual field loss, seizures, and other signs of white matter damage.

JC virus encephalopathy / JC virus-relat.normalized_text: JC virus encephalopathy / JC virus-related CNS infection
JC virus encephalopathy / JC virus-relat.description: A central nervous system infection caused by JC virus in immunocompromised patients. It may overlap clinically with PML and can cause focal deficits, seizures, and progressive neurological dysfunction.

Fingolimod-associated lymphopenia with o.description: Fingolimod can lower circulating lymphocytes and increase susceptibility to opportunistic infections. In an immunosuppressed patient, this may present with new neurological deficits due to a secondary CNS infection.

Multiple sclerosis relapse / demyelinati.description: An inflammatory recurrence of multiple sclerosis causing new or worsening neurological symptoms from CNS demyelination. It can produce visual, motor, and coordination abnormalities.

case: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

Fabry disease (Anderson-Fabry disease).description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, heart, and cornea.

Late-onset Fabry disease variant.description: A milder, later-presenting form of Fabry disease that may predominantly affect the heart and kidneys with fewer classic childhood manifestations.

Small fiber neuropathy.description: A disorder affecting small sensory and autonomic fibers, often causing burning pain, dysesthesia, and autonomic complaints.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy / other card.normalized_text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy / other cardiac source of chest discomfort
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy / other card.description: A cardiac disorder that can cause chest pain or discomfort due to structural heart disease, ischemia, or left ventricular outflow obstruction.

case: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma / liver a.description: A hematoma within the liver can become secondarily infected, leading to a hepatic abscess or infected collection. This often causes fever, leukocytosis, and abnormal liver tests.

Post-traumatic hepatic necrosis or ische.normalized_text: Post-traumatic hepatic necrosis or ischemic liver injury
Post-traumatic hepatic necrosis or ische.description: Blunt liver trauma can disrupt hepatic blood supply and cause tissue necrosis, inflammation, fever, leukocytosis, and elevated liver enzymes.

Hospital-acquired infection or sepsis un.normalized_text: Hospital-acquired infection or sepsis unrelated to the liver
Hospital-acquired infection or sepsis un.description: ICU patients are at risk for nosocomial infections such as pneumonia, catheter-related bloodstream infection, or urinary tract infection, which can cause fever and leukocytosis with nonspecific liver enzyme elevation.

Post-traumatic cholangitis or biliary ob.description: Trauma or compression from a hepatic hematoma can impair bile flow, leading to cholestasis or biliary infection, which may present with fever and abnormal liver tests.

case: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulos.description: A severe, usually drug-induced pustular eruption characterized by rapid onset of widespread sterile pustules on an erythematous base, fever, and neutrophilia; it often resolves after stopping the triggering agent.

Generalized Pustular Psoriasis.description: A severe psoriasis variant presenting with widespread sterile pustules, erythema, and systemic inflammation; it can resemble drug eruptions histologically and clinically.

Bullous Impetigo.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, producing flaccid bullae and pustules; microbiologic testing is typically positive.

Drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction.description: An adverse immune-mediated cutaneous reaction to a medication or contrast agent that can manifest with varied rashes, eosinophilia, and systemic findings.

case: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting սկսing the day before admission. He had dog bites to the hands and forearms 3 days earlier, head trauma from a rusty nail a few days earlier, and dental extractions 1–2 weeks earlier. Past history includes asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse with heavy recent use stopped 3 days prior. On exam he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with T 35.6°C, BP 154/102 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, RR 28/min, and O2 sat 100% on room air. Multiple lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks were present on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm purplish surrounding area; capillary refill was 5 seconds.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome.description: A hyperadrenergic state that occurs after abrupt reduction or cessation of heavy alcohol use, causing autonomic instability and gastrointestinal symptoms.
