Necrotizing soft tissue infection (e.g.,.normalized_text: Necrotizing soft tissue infection (e.g., necrotizing fasciitis) from dog bites
Necrotizing soft tissue infection (e.g.,.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening soft tissue infection that can follow traumatic skin breaches, including animal bites, and causes pain, skin discoloration, necrosis, and poor perfusion.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection.description: A zoonotic bacterial infection acquired from dog bites or saliva exposure that can cause severe systemic illness and soft tissue infection, especially after animal bites.

Tetanus.description: A toxin-mediated infection caused by Clostridium tetani entering through contaminated wounds, classically after puncture or contaminated injuries, leading to autonomic and neuromuscular symptoms.

Acute gastritis or peptic ulcer disease.normalized_text: Acute gastritis or peptic ulcer disease
Acute gastritis or peptic ulcer disease.description: Inflammation or ulceration of the gastric or duodenal mucosa that can cause epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, often associated with alcohol use.

case: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS syndrome (Mitochondrial Encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like Episodes)
MELAS syndrome (Mitochondrial Encephalom.description: A mitochondrial disorder, usually due to mtDNA mutations affecting oxidative phosphorylation, characterized by childhood-onset muscle weakness, lactic acidosis, and recurrent stroke-like neurologic episodes.

Mitochondrial myopathy.description: A group of disorders caused by impaired mitochondrial energy production leading predominantly to skeletal muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, and muscle wasting.

Mitochondrial tRNA Leu(UUR) mutation-ass.description: A specific mitochondrial disease caused by mutations in the MT-TL1 gene (tRNA leucine), often producing neuromuscular dysfunction, lactic acidosis, and neurologic deficits.

Stroke-like episodes secondary to mitoch.normalized_text: Stroke-like episodes secondary to mitochondrial disease
Stroke-like episodes secondary to mitoch.description: Recurrent acute neurologic deficits that mimic ischemic stroke but occur in mitochondrial disorders due to impaired cerebral energy metabolism rather than typical vascular occlusion.

case: A 29-year-old woman with a 7-week history of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea սկս after eating sushi. Three weeks later, she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and amber urine. Symptoms did not improve with methylprednisolone, hydroxyzine, or diphenoxylate-atropine. Prior labs showed elevated ALT 327 U/L, AST 104 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and CA 19-9 73 U/mL. History included anxiety and depression, with no medications or drug allergies. On exam, she was thin, jaundiced with scleral icterus, and had diffuse excoriations from scratching; vitals were stable aside from blood pressure 155/82 mm Hg.

Clonorchiasis (liver fluke infection).description: A parasitic infection caused by ingestion of raw or undercooked freshwater fish contaminated with Clonorchis species; it can involve the biliary tree and cause cholestatic hepatitis, biliary inflammation, and obstruction.

Extrahepatic biliary obstruction / chole.description: Obstruction of the common bile duct, often from gallstones, leading to cholestasis, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and right upper quadrant pain.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: A chronic inflammatory disease causing multifocal strictures of the bile ducts and progressive cholestatic liver injury, often associated with pruritus and jaundice.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: An immune-mediated liver inflammation that can cause elevated transaminases, jaundice, fatigue, and sometimes cholestatic symptoms.

Drug-induced liver injury.description: Liver damage caused by medications or supplements, which can present with hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed patterns of injury and may lead to jaundice and pruritus.

Acute viral hepatitis.description: Inflammation of the liver due to viral infection, often causing jaundice, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and elevated liver enzymes.

case: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

Rectal gallstone (choledocholithiasis/ga.normalized_text: Rectal gallstone (choledocholithiasis/gallstone lodged in the rectum)
Rectal gallstone (choledocholithiasis/ga.description: A gallstone that has migrated through the gastrointestinal tract and become impacted in the rectum, causing obstructive rectal symptoms and minor bleeding.

Rectal foreign body.description: An object retained in the rectum that can cause obstructive symptoms, foreign-body sensation, and rectal bleeding; it is often diagnosed and removed by endoscopy.

Fecal impaction.description: A large, hard mass of stool obstructs the rectum or distal colon, leading to constipation, a feeling of rectal fullness, and sometimes minor bleeding.

Crohn's disease with fistulizing complic.description: Crohn's disease can cause strictures, fistulas, and abnormal passage of intestinal contents, which may contribute to obstructive or unusual rectal findings.

case: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella out of the trochlear groove, usually laterally, often after twisting or minor trauma. It commonly causes sudden pain, swelling, inability to bear weight, and a feeling that the knee gave way.

Medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) in.description: The MPFL is the main soft tissue stabilizer preventing lateral patellar dislocation. Injury or tearing commonly occurs with a patellar dislocation and causes medial tenderness and knee instability.

Osteochondral fracture with intra-articu.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture with intra-articular loose body
Osteochondral fracture with intra-articu.description: An osteochondral injury involves cartilage and underlying bone, often after patellar dislocation. A fragment can become a loose body in the joint and cause mechanical symptoms such as locking, swelling, and pain.

Generalized joint hypermobility / hyperm.normalized_text: Generalized joint hypermobility / hypermobility spectrum disorder
Generalized joint hypermobility / hyperm.description: A condition characterized by increased joint laxity and a tendency toward joint instability or subluxation. It can predispose adolescents to patellar instability and soft tissue injury.

case: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by a triad of scarring alopecia of the scalp, non-scarring alopecia of axillary/pubic hair, and follicular keratotic papules on the trunk and limbs.

Lichen planopilaris.description: An inflammatory, scarring alopecia disorder in the lichen planus spectrum that causes perifollicular inflammation and hair loss, often with pruritus and scalp symptoms.

Follicular lichen planus.description: A variant of lichen planus involving hair follicles, producing keratotic follicular papules and sometimes pruritus; it can overlap with lichen planopilaris.

Pityriasis rubra pilaris.description: A papulosquamous disorder that can cause follicular hyperkeratotic papules, widespread scaling, and sometimes itching; severe forms may involve hair loss indirectly through inflammation.

Keratosis pilaris / keratosis pilaris va.description: A common follicular keratinization disorder that causes rough, spiny papules on the skin, usually on the arms, thighs, and trunk, and may be associated with mild itching.

case: 35-year-old woman with a history of preeclampsia during pregnancy 12 months earlier, requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks. After delivery, she developed poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Six months before admission, she developed fatigue, headaches, severe hypertension, and facial and pedal oedema. On presentation, she had severe hypertension, oedema, and renal failure. Examination showed pallor and blood pressure of 151/103 mmHg. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, reticulocytosis, schistocytes, proteinuria of 4.9 g/24h, hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coombs test. Liver enzymes were normal, and immunologic, viral, and antiphospholipid antibody tests were negative.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS.description: A complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy causing hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period.

Postpartum thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A broad clinical syndrome of microangiopathic hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury occurring after delivery, which can overlap with aHUS, TTP, or severe hypertensive disorders.

Malignant hypertension with thrombotic m.description: A severe hypertensive emergency that can damage small vessels and cause renal failure, proteinuria, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and retinal or neurologic symptoms.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, classically producing thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, neurologic findings, fever, and variable renal injury.

Preeclampsia/eclampsia spectrum with per.normalized_text: Preeclampsia/eclampsia spectrum with persistent postpartum renal disease
Preeclampsia/eclampsia spectrum with per.description: A hypertensive disorder of pregnancy that can cause hypertension, proteinuria, edema, and renal injury, sometimes with postpartum persistence or progression.

case: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.normalized_text: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract, commonly driven by activating KIT mutations. It often presents with occult or overt GI bleeding, anemia, abdominal mass, or incidental imaging findings.

Small bowel neoplasm causing occult/over.normalized_text: Small bowel neoplasm causing occult/overt gastrointestinal bleeding
Small bowel neoplasm causing occult/over.description: A broad category that includes tumors of the small intestine such as GIST, adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, and neuroendocrine tumors. These can present with bleeding, anemia, and a localized mass.

Small intestinal gastrointestinal bleedi.normalized_text: Small intestinal gastrointestinal bleeding from a submucosal tumor
Small intestinal gastrointestinal bleedi.description: A submucosal lesion in the small bowel can cause mucosal ulceration and bleeding, leading to iron-deficiency or acute blood-loss anemia and hemodynamic symptoms.

Small bowel adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can present with bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, or obstruction, and may appear as a focal bowel wall mass.

Small bowel lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the small intestine that may present with anemia, bleeding, abdominal mass, or nonspecific abdominal findings.

case: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Pancreatic cystic neoplasm.description: A tumor of the pancreas containing fluid-filled cystic spaces, such as serous or mucinous cystic neoplasms, which can present as an abdominal mass and digestive symptoms due to compression of nearby structures.

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of the pancreas that often presents late with vague abdominal symptoms, weight loss, digestive difficulty, or a palpable mass when advanced.

Chronic pancreatitis with pancreatic pse.description: Long-standing inflammation of the pancreas that can lead to maldigestion and the formation of a pseudocyst or inflammatory mass in the abdomen.

Gastric cancer.description: A malignant tumor of the stomach that can cause upper abdominal fullness, impaired digestion, and a palpable epigastric mass in advanced cases.

Mesenteric or omental cyst.description: A benign cystic lesion within the abdominal cavity that may present as a painless, palpable mass and nonspecific abdominal fullness.

case: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial p.description: A rare inherited blistering disorder that affects skin folds, causing recurrent painful, itchy erosions and crusted lesions that often worsen with heat, sweating, and friction.

Acanthosis nigricans.description: A skin condition characterized by dark, thickened, velvety plaques, usually in body folds, often associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and sometimes diabetes.

Intertrigo.description: Inflammation of skin folds caused by friction, moisture, and heat, sometimes complicated by secondary infection and skin breakdown.

Pseudofolliculitis barbae.description: An inflammatory skin condition caused by ingrown hairs after shaving, most often affecting the beard area and common in people with tightly curled hair.

case: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

Ovarian cyst.description: A fluid-filled sac arising from the ovary; many are benign and can present as a slowly enlarging pelvic mass with localized pain or tenderness.

Endometrioma.description: An ovarian cyst formed by ectopic endometrial tissue, often associated with pelvic pain and an adnexal mass in reproductive-age women.

Ovarian neoplasm.description: A benign or malignant tumor of the ovary that can present as a progressively enlarging pelvic mass, sometimes with pain or tenderness.

Tubo-ovarian abscess.description: A localized pelvic infection involving the ovary and fallopian tube, usually causing pelvic pain, tenderness, and often fever or systemic symptoms.

Ectopic pregnancy.description: Implantation of a pregnancy outside the uterine cavity, commonly presenting with pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness, and sometimes a mass.

case: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed lower limbs and para-spinal muscle spasms that progressed over 3 months. Her symptoms continued to progress and she became wheelchair-bound 6 months later. When reviewed at institution, she was severely disabled requiring regular IVIG treatments at a dose of 90g every 12 days. She was taking regular diazepam at a dose of 30mg per day and morphine up to 60mg a day to control pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The muscle spasms were severe enough to compromise her breathing and she required intermittent oxygen.

Stiff Person Syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive muscle stiffness, painful spasms, and exaggerated startle or reflex responses, often associated with antibodies such as anti-GAD and sometimes improved with IVIG or benzodiazepines.

Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigid.normalized_text: Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigid.description: A severe variant within the stiff-person spectrum disorder group, causing rigidity, spasms, hyperreflexia, and often prominent brainstem or autonomic involvement.

Tetanus.description: An acute toxin-mediated illness caused by Clostridium tetani leading to muscle rigidity, painful spasms, hyperreflexia, and respiratory compromise.

Spinal Cord Lesion/Myelopathy.description: A structural or inflammatory spinal cord disorder that can cause spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and progressive weakness or gait impairment.

Multiple Sclerosis.description: A chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause spasticity, hyperreflexia, and progressive disability.

case: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

Vasovagal syncope.description: A common fainting disorder caused by a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure, often triggered by stress, pain, or prolonged standing.

Orthostatic hypotension.description: A fall in blood pressure on standing that can cause dizziness, weakness, or fainting.

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity.description: An exaggerated reflex from the carotid sinus causing bradycardia and hypotension, which can lead to syncope, especially with neck movement or pressure.

Transient ischemic attack or recurrent c.normalized_text: Transient ischemic attack or recurrent cerebrovascular event
Transient ischemic attack or recurrent c.description: A temporary or permanent reduction in cerebral blood flow causing neurological symptoms; in some cases, this may be described by patients as collapse.

case: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab, originally from Greece. Four months before admission she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP/IP joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli, with anemia, leukopenia/neutropenia, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, ANA 1:640, low C4, positive cryoglobulins, and negative HIV, HBV, and HCV serologies. On admission after a burn from an electric heater, she had fever and pancytopenia; there was no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood film, cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, CMV PCR, and tuberculin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens seven months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).description: A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies that can cause prolonged fever, pancytopenia, anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and immune-complex phenomena. In Mediterranean regions it can mimic autoimmune disease and may be associated with positive cryoglobulins and low complement.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, classically producing purpura, arthralgia, low complement, and elevated rheumatoid factor, sometimes with neuropathy or renal disease.

Rheumatoid arthritis flare with extra-ar.normalized_text: Rheumatoid arthritis flare with extra-articular vasculitis
Rheumatoid arthritis flare with extra-ar.description: An autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that can present with joint pain and stiffness, high rheumatoid factor, and in severe cases rheumatoid vasculitis causing purpura and systemic inflammation.

Systemic lupus erythematosus.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause fever, cytopenias, positive ANA, low complement, arthralgia, and vasculitic skin lesions.

Drug-induced cytopenia or infection-rela.normalized_text: Drug-induced cytopenia or infection-related immunosuppression complication
Drug-induced cytopenia or infection-rela.description: Bone marrow suppression or opportunistic infection related to immunosuppressive therapy such as methotrexate and adalimumab can cause fever and cytopenias, sometimes with atypical inflammatory or infectious manifestations.

case: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum.description: A chronic inflammatory skin disorder classically associated with diabetes that causes slowly enlarging yellow-brown to red-brown plaques, often on the shins, with central atrophy and tenderness.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis that can present as annular papules or plaques, sometimes on the extremities, and may be associated with diabetes.

Dermatofibroma.description: A common benign fibrous skin nodule that often occurs on the legs and may appear brownish with a firm or depressed center.

Stasis dermatitis.description: An inflammatory skin condition caused by chronic venous insufficiency that can lead to brown discoloration and skin changes on the lower legs.

case: 14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking while swallowing սկսed after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by fear of eating, vomiting after trying ice cream, markedly reduced oral intake, and one day of sleeping most of the day. Mother also reported inspiratory stridor during sleep over the preceding few weeks. History includes infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training in childhood, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, keratosis pilaris, and eczema. On exam he was alert but anxious, with persistent involuntary burping, drooling, and dry oral mucosa; later exam showed hypertonic leg muscles and mildly positive left Chvostek sign. Neurologic exam, gait, strength, sensation, reflexes, and cranial nerves were otherwise normal.

Phagophobia (choking-related swallowing.description: Anxiety disorder marked by a fear of swallowing or choking, often triggered by a traumatic choking event and leading to avoidance of eating and drinking.

Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorde.description: An eating disorder characterized by avoidance or restriction of food intake that is not driven by body image concerns, often due to fear of choking, vomiting, or sensory aversion.

Eosinophilic esophagitis.description: A chronic allergic/inflammatory esophageal disease that can cause dysphagia, food impaction, vomiting, and feeding avoidance, especially in patients with atopic history.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease with lar.normalized_text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease with laryngopharyngeal reflux
Gastroesophageal reflux disease with lar.description: Reflux of gastric contents causing esophageal irritation and sometimes upper-airway symptoms such as stridor, throat discomfort, or feeding aversion.

Hypocalcemia causing neuromuscular irrit.description: Low serum calcium can cause muscle cramps, tetany, paresthesias, and facial nerve irritability; severe cases may cause stridor or spasms.

Upper airway disorder such as laryngomal.normalized_text: Upper airway disorder such as laryngomalacia or vocal cord dysfunction
Upper airway disorder such as laryngomal.description: Conditions causing inspiratory airway noise or stridor; laryngomalacia is usually congenital and vocal cord dysfunction can be episodic and anxiety-related.

case: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months earlier, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. She started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib 1 month before admission, and developed fever and nausea 1 day later, which resolved after temporary discontinuation and antipyretics. Fever recurred 2 weeks before admission. On presentation, she was febrile to 40.2°C, tachycardic, diaphoretic, ill appearing, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and no rash.

Dabrafenib/trametinib-associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse effect of BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, especially dabrafenib plus trametinib, characterized by recurrent fever with or without chills, dehydration, hypotension, or organ dysfunction, often improving when treatment is held.

Drug fever.description: A febrile reaction caused by a medication, usually without evidence of infection or another inflammatory source, often resolving after the offending drug is stopped.

Hepatobiliary toxicity from targeted the.description: Medication-related liver or biliary inflammation/injury that can present with fever and right upper quadrant discomfort, sometimes accompanied by systemic symptoms.

Occult infection in an immunocompromised.normalized_text: Occult infection in an immunocompromised oncology patient
Occult infection in an immunocompromised.description: An infectious process such as bacteremia, pneumonia, urinary infection, or intra-abdominal infection that can cause high fever and systemic symptoms in a patient with cancer or recent surgery.

Tumor fever.description: Fever caused by malignancy-related cytokine release, more often seen with active or advanced cancer and sometimes difficult to distinguish from infection.

case: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones. It commonly presents with right upper quadrant pain, a positive Murphy's sign, and cholestatic liver enzyme elevation.

Gallstone pancreatitis.description: Pancreatic inflammation triggered by gallstone obstruction of the common bile duct or ampulla. It often causes abdominal pain with elevated lipase and may be associated with transient liver enzyme abnormalities.

Choledocholithiasis.description: Presence of gallstones in the common bile duct, which can cause biliary obstruction and elevated cholestatic enzymes, sometimes with pain and intermittent symptoms.

Acalculous cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, often occurring in ill or hospitalized patients. It can present with right upper quadrant pain, tenderness, and signs of biliary inflammation.

case: 13-year-old boy with progressive dysphagia since age 11, muscle weakness, severe fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. History includes recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, progressive hyperpigmentation from age 2, episodes of hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia leading to diagnosis of Addison’s disease at age 4, and deficient tear production since infancy. He also had bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias at birth, later global developmental delay with mild intellectual disability. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal muscle wasting and weakness in the arms, milder pyramidal weakness in the legs, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Labs showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.

Triple A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome, AA.description: A rare autosomal recessive disorder classically causing alacrima, achalasia, and adrenal insufficiency, often with progressive neurologic involvement such as neuropathy, pyramidal signs, and cerebellar features.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy / adrenomy.description: A peroxisomal disorder that can cause primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive neurologic dysfunction, including spasticity, ataxia, neuropathy, and developmental or cognitive issues.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: An inherited disorder of ACTH receptor signaling or adrenal steroidogenesis causing isolated cortisol deficiency with high ACTH, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, and crisis episodes in childhood.

Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.description: A lipid storage disorder due to sterol 27-hydroxylase deficiency, causing progressive neurologic disease, developmental problems, ataxia, pyramidal signs, and sometimes early cataracts or gastrointestinal symptoms.

Mitochondrial disorder with multisystem.description: A group of inherited energy metabolism disorders that can affect the brain, muscles, endocrine organs, and gastrointestinal tract, often producing progressive weakness, ataxia, developmental delay, and failure to thrive.

case: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of stage IV invasive ductal breast cancer (ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative) metastatic to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy, multiple systemic therapies, and stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. Recently on anastrozole for 3 months and paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found disoriented with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. Exam showed her awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without focal neurologic deficits initially; vital signs were notable for mild tachycardia, normal blood pressure, and no fever. Baseline brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy.description: Elevated blood calcium due to cancer, often from bone metastases or tumor-mediated bone resorption, causing neurocognitive slowing, weakness, dehydration, and reduced responsiveness.

Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.description: Diffuse spread of cancer cells to the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, which can cause altered mental status, multifocal neurologic deficits, and rapidly progressive neurologic decline.

Paraneoplastic encephalopathy / autoimmu.description: Immune-mediated brain dysfunction associated with cancer that can present with confusion, behavioral changes, decreased consciousness, and sometimes weakness or seizures.

Metastatic brain disease.description: Direct spread of breast cancer to the brain, which can cause altered mental status, weakness, and other focal or generalized neurologic symptoms.

Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy.description: Diffuse brain dysfunction caused by systemic metabolic disturbances, medication effects, or organ dysfunction, leading to confusion, reduced alertness, and impaired responsiveness.

case: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness in all four extremities, sensory changes, and subsequent urinary difficulty. Exam showed hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and asymmetric motor weakness (MRC 2 on the right, MRC 4 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature below C4, worse on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, worse on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal; ACE was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study showed no abnormalities.

Cervical transverse myelitis.description: An inflammatory spinal cord syndrome causing motor weakness, sensory loss, and autonomic dysfunction below a spinal level.

Neurosarcoidosis with spinal cord involv.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disorder that can affect the central nervous system, including the spinal cord, producing myelopathy and autonomic symptoms.

Cervical spinal cord compressive myelopa.description: Mechanical compression of the cervical spinal cord, such as from spondylosis, disc disease, or other structural lesions, causing upper motor neuron signs and sensory deficits.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that can cause severe longitudinal spinal cord inflammation leading to weakness, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction.

Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord invo.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord involvement
Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord invo.description: A demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can present with myelopathic symptoms from cervical cord lesions.

case: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum শুরু after a cold. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, dyspnea, or initial chest pain. He received unknown IV treatment at a local clinic without improvement. Cough worsened 7 days before admission, especially at night with sleep disturbance, and was sometimes accompanied by right-sided chest pain. Past history unremarkable; smokes about 10 cigarettes/day for over 10 years, no alcohol use. Exam: T 36.2℃, P 112/min, R 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg. Chest exam showed symmetric thorax and movements, symmetric vocal fremitus, clear percussion, coarse breath sounds bilaterally, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung, without dry rales or pleural friction rub.

Acute bronchitis.description: Inflammation of the bronchi, usually following a viral upper respiratory infection, causing cough with or without sputum and abnormal breath sounds.

Community-acquired pneumonia.description: An infection of the lung parenchyma that can cause cough, sputum production, focal crackles, and chest pain.

Post-infectious cough.description: A lingering cough that persists for weeks after a respiratory infection due to airway hypersensitivity and inflammation.

Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis.description: A flare of chronic airway inflammation, often in smokers, with increased cough and sputum production.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often presenting with persistent cough and sometimes sputum or chest discomfort.

case: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

Dirofilariasis (subcutaneous infection w.description: A zoonotic filarial infection transmitted by mosquitoes, often causing a solitary or migrating painless subcutaneous nodule, especially in people exposed to dogs and outdoor environments.

Subcutaneous zoonotic filariasis due to.normalized_text: Subcutaneous zoonotic filariasis due to other filarial parasites
Subcutaneous zoonotic filariasis due to.description: A group of filarial infections acquired from animal reservoirs that can present as localized subcutaneous nodules with minimal systemic inflammation.

Panniculitis of noninfectious origin.description: Inflammation of subcutaneous fat that can form nodules, sometimes firm and well-defined, but usually accompanied by tenderness or inflammatory signs.

Subcutaneous cyst or benign soft tissue.normalized_text: Subcutaneous cyst or benign soft tissue tumor
Subcutaneous cyst or benign soft tissue.description: Benign localized masses such as epidermoid cysts, lipoma, or fibrous nodules can present as painless subcutaneous lumps.

case: 66-year-old man with progressive neurologic symptoms beginning around 2000, including recurrent unexplained falls, blurred vision, photophobia, imbalance, and gait unsteadiness. In 2003 he was noted to have irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes, slow and limited voluntary vertical eye movements, slow horizontal gaze with bilateral adduction paresis, and preserved convergence. He also developed slowed and inaccurate distal rapid alternating movements and backward falls. Over time he worsened with frequent falls requiring a cane, retrocollis, dysarthria, inability to look down, and dysphagia. By March 2007, he had repeated aspirations and severe ocular motility limitation with absent vertical and medial eye movements, impaired convergence, absent Bell’s phenomenon, optokinetic nystagmus, and caloric- or doll’s eye-evoked nystagmus. He also had severe nuchal rigidity, axial rigidity, inability to sit independently, and repeated backward falls.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), Ri.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by early postural instability, frequent falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, axial rigidity, dysarthria, and dysphagia.

Multiple system atrophy, cerebellar/PSP-.description: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing autonomic failure, parkinsonism, cerebellar signs, and sometimes prominent gait and balance problems; some variants can resemble PSP.

Parkinson-plus syndrome with predominant.normalized_text: Parkinson-plus syndrome with predominant brainstem ocular motor involvement
Parkinson-plus syndrome with predominant.description: A clinical category of atypical parkinsonian syndromes that includes disorders with early postural instability, axial rigidity, and abnormal eye movements, often due to brainstem degeneration.

case: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: A fungal infection of the central nervous system, classically seen in advanced HIV/AIDS, causing subacute meningitis with raised intracranial pressure.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often presenting with subacute fever, headache, meningismus, and abnormal CSF with lymphocytic predominance.

Viral meningitis/meningoencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes extending to the brain, caused by viruses such as enteroviruses, HSV, or VZV; often produces lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis.

Bacterial meningitis.description: An acute infection of the meninges caused by bacteria, usually producing fever, headache, neck stiffness, and neutrophilic CSF with low glucose.

Neurosyphilis.description: Central nervous system infection by Treponema pallidum, which can cause meningitis-like symptoms and lymphocytic CSF abnormalities, especially in people with HIV.

case: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (left media.normalized_text: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (left medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (left media.description: A brainstem eye-movement disorder caused by damage to the medial longitudinal fasciculus, leading to impaired adduction of the affected eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye.

Brainstem ischemic stroke.description: An acute loss of blood flow to the brainstem that can produce isolated ocular motor findings, especially if the lesion involves the pons or midbrain pathways controlling eye movements.

Microvascular cranial nerve palsy.description: Ischemic dysfunction of an ocular motor cranial nerve, usually in older adults with vascular risk factors, causing binocular diplopia and ocular motility deficits.

Left medial rectus weakness due to oculo.normalized_text: Left medial rectus weakness due to oculomotor nerve palsy
Left medial rectus weakness due to oculo.description: A palsy of the third cranial nerve can impair adduction, though it usually also affects other eye movements and may be associated with ptosis or pupillary abnormalities.

Ocular myasthenia gravis.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can cause fluctuating diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, often without sensory loss or other neurological deficits.

case: 35-day-old male infant with 2 days of worsening illness: previously well at routine exam, then developed fussiness, pallor, warmth, vomiting, tachycardia, fever, mottled skin, and respiratory distress on admission. Born at 37.5 weeks via cesarean section as a fraternal twin; previously healthy and fed breast milk plus formula. Exam showed temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, pale listless appearance, mottled cool extremities, a holosystolic-flow murmur, and spleen palpable 2–3 cm below the costal margin. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts.

Neonatal sepsis.description: A serious systemic bacterial infection in a young infant that can cause fever, poor perfusion, respiratory distress, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Urinary tract infection / acute pyelonep.description: An infection of the urinary tract or kidneys that in young infants may present nonspecifically with fever, vomiting, irritability, and signs of systemic illness.

Hemolytic anemia.description: Destruction of red blood cells causing pallor, tachycardia, possible dark urine from hemoglobinuria, and splenic enlargement.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome.description: A condition characterized by hemolytic anemia, kidney injury, and low platelets, often following an infection; it can cause hematuria and abnormal urine findings.

Congestive heart failure due to congenit.normalized_text: Congestive heart failure due to congenital heart disease
Congestive heart failure due to congenit.description: Poor cardiac function from an underlying structural heart defect can cause tachycardia, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, and a murmur in infants.

case: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

Locally recurrent prostate adenocarcinom.normalized_text: Locally recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal invasion
Locally recurrent prostate adenocarcinom.description: Return of prostate cancer after prior treatment, with local spread into nearby structures such as the rectum, which can cause pelvic or rectal pain and obstructive symptoms.

Rectal or colorectal carcinoma.description: A malignant tumor arising in the rectum or colon that can present with rectal pain, tenesmus, constitutional symptoms, and weight loss.

Perirectal abscess or chronic anorectal.normalized_text: Perirectal abscess or chronic anorectal infection
Perirectal abscess or chronic anorectal.description: A localized infection near the anus or rectum that can cause significant rectal pain and painful defecatory urgency; systemic symptoms may occur if severe or prolonged.

Radiation proctitis.description: Inflammation and injury of the rectum after pelvic radiation, leading to rectal discomfort, urgency, tenesmus, and sometimes bleeding.

Metastatic malignancy causing cancer-rel.description: Advanced cancer with systemic effects such as involuntary weight loss, anorexia, and fatigue; pelvic metastasis or local recurrence could also produce pain.

case: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the upper legs followed by acute inability to lift his legs or stand on the day of presentation, with weakness in the arms. For several months আগে he had difficulty sleeping, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremors. He had started an herbal supplement 4 days before presentation. On examination, he had bilateral conjunctival injection, proximal muscle weakness (3/5 in lower extremities, 4/5 in upper extremities), 3+ patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis, elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, mildly elevated creatine kinase and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.description: An acute, reversible episode of flaccid muscle weakness caused by severe hypokalemia in the setting of thyrotoxicosis, often triggered by stress, exercise, or carbohydrate intake.

Hyperthyroidism (likely Graves disease).description: An autoimmune thyroid disorder causing excess thyroid hormone production, with symptoms such as weight loss, tremor, insomnia, and increased gastrointestinal motility.

Hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: A disorder characterized by episodic flaccid muscle weakness associated with low serum potassium, often due to ion channel dysfunction or secondary causes.

Herbal supplement-induced thyrotoxicosis.description: Thyrotoxicosis caused by ingestion of supplements contaminated with thyroid hormone or iodine-containing substances, which can precipitate hyperthyroid symptoms and periodic paralysis.

case: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.

Congenital epulis.description: A rare benign congenital soft-tissue mass of the oral cavity, usually present at birth and often arising from the alveolar ridge.

Oral dermoid cyst.description: A benign developmental cyst that can present as a slow-growing mass in the floor of the mouth or oral cavity, sometimes congenital or long-standing.

Lymphatic malformation (lymphangioma).description: A congenital benign malformation of lymphatic vessels that can appear as a persistent oral mass and may cause local irritation or hygiene problems.

Congenital oral hamartoma.description: A benign overgrowth of normal tissues that is present from birth and usually causes limited symptoms unless it interferes with oral hygiene or function.

Accessory oral tissue / congenital soft.normalized_text: Accessory oral tissue / congenital soft tissue tag
Accessory oral tissue / congenital soft.description: A benign congenital extra tissue growth in the oral cavity that may remain stable over time and mainly causes cosmetic or hygiene-related issues.

case: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar radiculopathy due to herniated in.normalized_text: Lumbar radiculopathy due to herniated intervertebral disc
Lumbar radiculopathy due to herniated in.description: Compression or irritation of a lumbar nerve root, often from a disc herniation, causing back pain that radiates into the leg along with weakness or sensory symptoms.

Sciatica.description: Pain caused by irritation of the sciatic nerve or its roots, typically producing low back pain that radiates down one leg and may be accompanied by weakness.

Lumbar spinal stenosis.description: Narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back that can compress nerve roots and cause back pain, leg pain, and weakness.

Mechanical low back pain with referred p.normalized_text: Mechanical low back pain with referred pain
Mechanical low back pain with referred p.description: Musculoskeletal back pain from strain or degenerative changes, sometimes producing referred pain into the leg without true nerve root involvement.

Cauda equina syndrome.description: Compression of the nerve roots in the lower spinal canal, a neurological emergency that can cause back pain, leg weakness, sensory changes, and bowel or bladder dysfunction.

case: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A disorder defined by persistent marked eosinophilia that causes organ damage, commonly affecting the heart, nervous system, skin, and lungs, without an identifiable secondary cause.

Eosinophilic myocarditis.description: An inflammatory heart disease caused by eosinophilic infiltration of the myocardium, leading to myocardial injury, elevated cardiac biomarkers, arrhythmias, or heart failure.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A small- to medium-vessel vasculitis characterized by asthma, sinus disease, eosinophilia, and systemic organ involvement including the heart and nervous system.

Parasitic eosinophilic infection with CN.normalized_text: Parasitic eosinophilic infection with CNS and cardiac involvement
Parasitic eosinophilic infection with CN.description: Certain helminthic infections can cause severe eosinophilia and can involve the brain or heart, producing neurologic symptoms and myocardial injury.

Eosinophilic leukemia / myeloproliferati.description: A clonal hematologic disorder in which abnormal eosinophil proliferation leads to persistent eosinophilia and end-organ damage, including cardiac and neurologic complications.

case: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving lymph nodes, lungs, skin, or eyes and sometimes associated with elevated ACE levels and PET-avid lesions.

Sarcoid-like reaction associated with ma.description: A noninfectious granulomatous reaction that can occur in patients with cancer or after cancer treatment, producing PET-avid lesions that may mimic recurrence or metastasis.

Breast cancer recurrence or metastasis.description: Return or spread of the original breast cancer, which can present as abnormal FDG-PET uptake and may be accompanied by cytopenias if there is bone marrow involvement.

Tuberculosis.description: An infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can cause granulomatous disease and FDG-PET abnormalities, sometimes mimicking malignancy or sarcoidosis.

case: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia and elevated ESR. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia on perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination was normal, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 99 g/L, ESR 120 mm/h, mildly elevated creatinine 110 μmol/L, calcium 2.81 mmol/L, and LDH 333 U/L. Further testing revealed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, elevated β₂-microglobulin 6.3 mg/L, free kappa light chains 1,400 mg/L with kappa/lambda ratio 280, and urinary Bence-Jones protein (kappa); 24-hour urine protein was normal.

Multiple myeloma.description: A malignant plasma cell disorder characterized by clonal immunoglobulin production and end-organ damage such as anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, or bone disease.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic plasma cell dyscrasia with significant monoclonal protein or marrow involvement but without clear myeloma-defining end-organ damage.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A benign premalignant plasma cell condition with a small monoclonal protein and no end-organ damage.

Light chain multiple myeloma / kappa lig.normalized_text: Light chain multiple myeloma / kappa light-chain predominant plasma cell dyscrasia
Light chain multiple myeloma / kappa lig.description: A plasma cell neoplasm in which excess free light chains are produced, often causing renal injury and other myeloma-related complications.

case: 20-year-old male with 3 years of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. He reported decreased facial hair growth, small testicles, occasional morning erections, and no sexual activity. Four years earlier he had polydipsia, increased fluid intake, and urinary frequency, recently improved. He also had blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertional headaches, recent constipation, and a past history of generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic and focal right leg seizures from ages 6–13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14. Examination showed minimal facial hair, bilateral breast enlargement without masses, retraction, or discharge, and small testicles; also noted were a small posterior anal fissure and a coccygeal lump with central punctum.

Prolactinoma (pituitary lactotroph adeno.description: A prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor that can cause hypogonadism, gynecomastia, reduced libido, headaches, and visual symptoms from mass effect.

Nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma ca.description: A pituitary tumor that does not secrete hormones but may compress normal pituitary tissue and nearby structures, leading to low gonadal hormones, visual problems, and headaches.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A benign sellar/suprasellar tumor that often presents with headaches, visual changes, and pituitary hormone deficiencies, and may also cause diabetes insipidus if the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary is involved.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.description: A condition in which the hypothalamus or pituitary fails to stimulate the testes adequately, leading to low testosterone, delayed or incomplete sexual development, and sometimes gynecomastia.

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).description: A chromosomal disorder in males characterized by primary testicular failure, small testes, sparse facial/body hair, gynecomastia, and infertility.

case: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Infective endocarditis of the aortic val.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis of the aortic valve due to MRSA
Infective endocarditis of the aortic val.description: A bacterial infection of the endocardial surface, often involving heart valves, causing persistent bacteremia, fever, new or changing murmurs, and embolic complications.

Septic embolic ischemic stroke.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolization of infected material, commonly from infective endocarditis, leading to focal neurologic deficits and altered consciousness.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: Presence of MRSA in the bloodstream, which can cause systemic inflammatory symptoms and seed distant sites such as the heart, brain, and bones.

Disseminated staphylococcal infection wi.normalized_text: Disseminated staphylococcal infection with metastatic foci (discitis/psoas abscess and possible endocardial involvement)
Disseminated staphylococcal infection wi.description: A systemic Staphylococcus aureus infection that spreads to multiple sites, producing vertebral or soft tissue abscesses and potentially infective endocarditis with embolic complications.

case: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, leading to glycogen accumulation in muscle and heart; infantile forms often present with cardiomyopathy, elevated CK, and weakness, and can be detected by newborn screening before symptoms appear.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A milder form of GAA deficiency that typically presents later in childhood or adulthood with progressive limb-girdle weakness and respiratory involvement, usually without severe early cardiomyopathy.

Pompe disease pseudodeficiency / false-p.normalized_text: Pompe disease pseudodeficiency / false-positive newborn screening for GAA deficiency
Pompe disease pseudodeficiency / false-p.description: A condition in which GAA enzyme activity appears low on screening assays but does not reflect true lysosomal disease; it can cause false-positive newborn screening results.

case: 6-year-old girl with 1 year of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain after a fall on her left hand, including rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, limping, and intermittent fever up to 39.8°C. The day before admission, she developed periorbital swelling, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination, she was febrile (38.7°C), had bilateral periorbital discoloration, a soft nontender abdomen, slight limping, and pain with external rotation of the right hip. Past history included infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis.

Neuroblastoma.description: A malignant tumor of the sympathetic nervous system, usually arising from the adrenal gland or paraspinal ganglia, often presenting with abdominal mass, bone pain, fever, and periorbital ecchymosis from metastatic spread.

Acute leukemia (especially acute lymphob.description: A blood and bone marrow cancer that can cause bone pain, limp, fever, and sometimes bruising or systemic symptoms due to marrow infiltration and cytopenias.

Ewing sarcoma.description: A malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents that commonly causes localized bone pain, swelling, limp, and fever, and may mimic infection.

Osteomyelitis / septic arthritis.description: An infection of bone or joint that can cause localized pain, limp, fever, and pain with movement of the affected joint.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A clonal histiocytic disorder that can affect bone and cause pain, swelling, limp, and sometimes systemic symptoms such as fever.

case: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

Cellulitis.description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue that causes localized redness, warmth, swelling, and tenderness.

Skin abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in the skin or soft tissue, often presenting as a painful, swollen, erythematous mass.

Pilonidal abscess.description: An infected cyst or abscess near the natal cleft that can cause pain, swelling, and redness in the buttock or sacrococcygeal area.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, severe infection of the soft tissues that can present with pain, swelling, and skin erythema, often requiring urgent treatment.

case: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease with s.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerodermoid features
Chronic graft-versus-host disease with s.description: An immune-mediated complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation in which donor T cells attack host tissues, often affecting skin, liver, eyes, and mouth; it can cause inflammatory or sclerotic skin changes and joint/fascial tightness.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin findings, often photo-distributed rashes; it may be associated with elevated muscle enzymes and autoimmune serologies.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus.description: A photosensitive autoimmune skin disease associated with anti-Ro/SSA antibodies and ANA positivity, causing non-scarring annular or papulosquamous eruptions on sun-exposed and sometimes widespread areas.

Scleroderma-spectrum disease / systemic.normalized_text: Scleroderma-spectrum disease / systemic sclerosis-like overlap syndrome
Scleroderma-spectrum disease / systemic.description: A connective tissue disorder causing skin thickening and tightening, microvascular dysfunction, and sometimes internal organ involvement; overlap syndromes can produce positive ANA and limited joint mobility.

Porphyria cutanea tarda.description: A disorder of heme synthesis causing photosensitivity and skin fragility, classically with blistering on sun-exposed areas and elevated liver enzymes; it is often associated with liver disease or iron overload.

case: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

Acquired perforating dermatosis.description: A chronic skin disorder seen mainly in patients with chronic kidney disease or diabetes, characterized by itchy papules or nodules with transepidermal elimination of altered dermal material.

Prurigo nodularis.description: A chronic itchy skin condition with firm papules or nodules caused by the itch-scratch cycle, often associated with systemic pruritus including uremia.

Uremic pruritus.description: Generalized itching associated with advanced chronic kidney disease and dialysis, often leading to excoriations and secondary pruritic skin lesions.

Actinic prurigo.description: A chronic photodermatosis causing intensely itchy papules, nodules, and excoriations on sun-exposed skin, usually triggered or worsened by ultraviolet exposure.

Lichen simplex chronicus.description: A localized thickening of the skin caused by repeated scratching or rubbing, usually driven by chronic pruritus.

case: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst presented with left arm pain, frontal headache, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute low back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission, she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, GCS 15, no fever, and no meningism. Labs showed leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF and electromyography were normal.

Acute transverse myelitis.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord that can cause rapidly progressive weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder dysfunction below the affected level.

Spinal epidural abscess.description: A collection of pus in the epidural space that compresses the spinal cord and can cause back pain, progressive neurologic deficits, and bladder symptoms; fever may or may not be present early.

Spinal cord infarction.description: Sudden ischemic injury to the spinal cord, often producing acute pain followed by weakness, sensory level abnormalities, and autonomic dysfunction such as urinary retention.

Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord invo.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord involvement
Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord invo.description: A demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause relapsing neurologic symptoms including sensory changes, weakness, and bladder dysfunction.

Brown-Séquard syndrome due to cervical o.normalized_text: Brown-Séquard syndrome due to cervical or thoracic spinal cord lesion
Brown-Séquard syndrome due to cervical o.description: A hemicord syndrome caused by compression or injury to one side of the spinal cord, leading to asymmetric weakness and dissociated sensory loss below the lesion.

case: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL.description: An aggressive acute leukemia of immature T-cell precursors, often presenting with very high blast counts, cytopenias, and a T-cell immunophenotype (e.g., CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7).

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, T-cell lin.description: A rapidly progressive malignancy of lymphoid precursors in the bone marrow and blood; in T-lineage disease, blasts express pan-T markers and usually lack B-cell and myeloid markers.

Acute leukemia of T-cell immunophenotype.normalized_text: Acute leukemia of T-cell immunophenotype, unspecified subtype
Acute leukemia of T-cell immunophenotype.description: An acute hematologic malignancy characterized by circulating blasts and marrow failure, with immunophenotyping indicating T-lineage, but without enough morphologic or genetic detail to fully classify the exact entity.

Leukostasis due to hyperleukocytic acute.normalized_text: Leukostasis due to hyperleukocytic acute leukemia
Leukostasis due to hyperleukocytic acute.description: A complication of acute leukemia in which very high white blood cell and blast counts impair microcirculation, causing headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and other organ symptoms.

case: A 36-year-old Chinese man presented with a 1-month history of persistent fever. He was previously healthy with no significant past medical history, specifically no prior TB infections, chronic illnesses, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune diseases. He was not taking any regular prescription medications and had not travelled abroad. On admission, vital signs showed temperature 37.2°C, heart rate 119 beats/min, blood pressure 90/48 mmHg, respiration rate 38 breaths/min with oxygen saturation 88%. Physical examination revealed an acutely ill appearance and pulmonary rales in both lungs. He presented with persistent fever, pancytopenia, and hyperferritinemia with clinical deterioration including acute respiratory failure.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by excessive immune activation, often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease, leading to prolonged fever, cytopenias, high ferritin, and multi-organ dysfunction.

Severe sepsis / septic shock.description: A life-threatening systemic infection with organ dysfunction and circulatory compromise, commonly presenting with fever, tachycardia, hypotension, respiratory distress, and sometimes cytopenias.

Acute leukemia.description: A malignant proliferation of immature blood cells in the bone marrow that can cause fever, pancytopenia, weakness, and severe complications from marrow failure or infection.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: A widespread form of tuberculosis that can produce prolonged fever, constitutional illness, cytopenias, and respiratory involvement, especially in severe systemic disease.

Adult-onset Still's disease.description: An autoinflammatory disorder characterized by high spiking fevers, systemic inflammation, and sometimes very elevated ferritin; severe cases can overlap with HLH.

case: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

Melioidosis (central nervous system invo.description: A severe infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired from soil or water in tropical regions. It can cause bacteremia, pneumonia, skin lesions, and, less commonly, brain abscesses or encephalitis with focal neurologic deficits.

Bacterial meningitis/meningoencephalitis.description: Acute infection of the meninges and brain tissue by bacteria, often presenting with fever, altered mental status, focal deficits, and cerebrospinal fluid inflammation dominated by neutrophils.

Leptospirosis with neurologic involvemen.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira species, acquired from contaminated water or animal urine. Severe cases can cause fever, rash, meningitis/encephalitis, and multiorgan involvement.

Arboviral encephalitis (e.g., dengue-ass.normalized_text: Arboviral encephalitis (e.g., dengue-associated encephalitis or another mosquito-borne viral encephalitis)
Arboviral encephalitis (e.g., dengue-ass.description: A viral brain infection transmitted by mosquitoes that can cause fever, rash, encephalopathy, and sometimes focal neurologic signs. Some arboviral infections may produce mild CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein.

Herpes simplex encephalitis.description: A life-threatening viral infection of the brain that often causes fever, altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits, and CSF inflammation. It can present with rapid neurologic decline.

case: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved over the past 3 years on weekly adalimumab, presented with 3 weeks of upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, chills).
